items.title: Model Hardware Standard: agents get a driver layer for the physical lab
items.summary: Anthropic's MHS research preview is not a robot and not a new model. It is a shared interface so agents can discover, describe, and operate programmable devices — with the hard problems still sitting in safety, spatial reasoning, and who writes the drivers.
items.body: MHS is a standardized hardware driver and discovery layer, not a new Claude model and not a general-purpose robot. It only works today on devices that already have a programmable interface. Paper-manual instruments are explicitly out of scope until vendors ship drivers. Control paths are MCP, CLI, and code/API files. The AI piece is optional for issuing commands; it is the point of the product story. Early evidence is partner-reported (Genentech, UW, CMU, Janelia, QuEra, Tetsuwan) plus a named vendor list. Independent replication is not in the public record yet. Safety is the gating item for open source: Anthropic says it will use the preview to build physical-world evaluations before releasing the spec. On 27 August 2026 Anthropic published 'Previewing the Model Hardware Standard,' opening a research preview to a first group of scientific labs and advanced manufacturers. The post states that MHS development began as a collaboration between Alek Kemeny on Anthropic's Beneficial Deployments team and Arco Bast, then a postdoctoral scientist at HHMI Janelia Research Campus, who needed a common interface for a multi-vendor brain-imaging rig. Anthropic claims a typical lab or factory integration that takes weeks or months can be reduced to hours or minutes, because devices currently do not share a common way to talk to each other or to an agent. The technical proposal is a driver with simple primitives (read/write style commands), natural-language tags for physical characteristics and safety limits, and a generated reference file the agent can use on devices it has not seen before. After devices are connected, an agent can sequence instruments, monitor results, and — for long-running or high-rate work — compile driver commands into code files so the hardware loop does not wait on model inference at every step. CNBC reported the same day, quoting Elizabeth Kelly that the work was built for science with enterprise and industry upside. Ars Technica independently described the same architecture and noted that a common machine interface does not, by itself, require an AI model. For a year, 'agentic AI' has mostly meant tools inside a computer: files, browsers, APIs, tickets. MHS is an attempt to reuse that tool-calling pattern on microscopes, liquid handlers, robotic arms, and lasers. If a model-agnostic hardware driver layer actually spreads, the bottleneck moves from 'can the model call a unique vendor SDK' to 'who certifies the driver, who sets the safety limits, and who audits the command log.' That is a systems story, not a chatbot story. Labs are a sharp test case. They already have programmable instruments, expensive integration work, and a culture of writing down procedures. They are also unforgiving of spatial mistakes, sample loss, and collision. The competitive map matters: NVIDIA is selling a vertically integrated physical-AI stack (simulation, world models, Jetson, Isaac). Anthropic is selling an interface. Those are different bets. One can win without the other dying. Open-sourcing, if it happens, would put MHS on the same path Anthropic took with MCP in 2024. Preview-only standards often stall at the partner-list stage. That is the thing to watch, not the launch video.

items.title: Anthropic opens a research preview of the Model Hardware Standard
items.summary: Anthropic published a primary announcement that MHS is in research preview with scientific labs and advanced manufacturers. The standard is model-agnostic, talks to existing programmable interfaces, and is intended to be open-sourced after safety work with partners.
items.body: This is the originating signal for the current edition. It is a company announcement, not an independent audit of the standard. The claims to carry forward are: research-preview status, programmable-interface requirement, model-agnostic access via MCP/CLI/API, origin at HHMI Janelia, and an explicit plan to open-source later — not immediately.

items.title: Independent write-up: MHS as a common driver layer for physical agents
items.summary: Kyle Orland's Ars Technica report restates the integration problem MHS claims to solve and notes that a common machine interface does not require an AI model — CLI and API control exist without one. MCP is the path that adds natural-language orchestration.
items.body: Useful as a second source because it separates the interoperability claim from the AI-agent claim. Keep that distinction in every briefing that cites MHS.

items.title: CNBC: Anthropic frames MHS as USB-C for machines, with an industrial follow-on
items.summary: Ashley Capoot's CNBC piece quotes Elizabeth Kelly on science-first intent with enterprise upside, and notes Anthropic's hardware and silicon hiring. Those hiring claims are attributed to LinkedIn/CNBC, not to the MHS specification itself.
items.body: Treat industrial-strategy color as context, not as evidence that MHS is a shipping product. The specification is still a partner preview.

items.title: Hugging Face is adding MHS support in LeRobot
items.summary: The Anthropic announcement says Hugging Face is adding MHS support in LeRobot, its robotics library. That is a vendor-reported adoption signal, not a reviewed pull request or release note from Hugging Face.
items.body: Next verification step: a Hugging Face primary source (docs, changelog, or repository change) that MHS drivers actually landed. Until then this stays a reported signal, not a verified product event.

items.title: Raspberry Pi: camera MHS driver tests, broader product integration planned
items.summary: Anthropic says Raspberry Pi is enabling MHS integration across a number of products following tests of a Camera MHS Driver. This is still an Anthropic-reported partner claim.
items.body: If confirmed on Raspberry Pi's own channels, this would be the clearest hobbyist/education path for MHS — and a different adoption surface than industrial arms or liquid handlers.

items.title: QuEra: agent-written laser lock recovers 99.3% of the time in MHS tests
items.summary: Anthropic reports that QuEra used MHS so an agent could control parts of a quantum laser system and recover laser lock 99.3% of the time without human intervention. The number is striking and needs a QuEra-side write-up before it is treated as a measured result rather than a partner anecdote.
items.body: Keep the figure attached to its source. Do not generalize from one laser-lock controller to 'AI runs quantum computers.'

items.body: No authored briefing has been published yet. Physical-AI control planes are a future cybersecurity story: once agents can issue hardware commands, the security boundary moves from the chat window to the lab floor.

items.title: Physical AI interface layer

items.body: This is not a complete map of physical AI. It is the interface-layer slice that currently has sourced coverage.

items.title: Windows Infrastructure Lab
items.summary: Windows Server, Active Directory, DNS, DHCP, Group Policy, domain authentication, organizational units and Windows client infrastructure.
items.body: A small-business style Windows environment built around Windows Server 2022. DC01 provides Active Directory and DNS for the corp.lab domain. CLIENT01 was installed, configured to use DC01 for DNS, joined to the domain, authenticated with a domain account and placed into the Workstations OU. A Workstation Baseline GPO was created and linked, and a successful policy refresh was performed. Live deployment was paused before the final DHCP/file-service expansion because the host reached its practical RAM and CPU limits. The repository retains the reconstruction procedures for DHCP, file services, permissions and deeper GPO verification.

items.title: Networking Lab
items.summary: Practical networking work covering TCP/IP, IPv4 and IPv6, DHCP, DNS, NAT, routing, VLANs, firewalling, packet analysis and network diagnostics.
items.body: A practical networking environment covering TCP/IP, IPv4 and IPv6, DHCP, DNS, NAT, routing, VLANs, firewalling, network services, packet analysis and diagnostics. Reference material is maintained alongside experiments so concepts, configurations and observed behaviour can be traced back to actual lab work. Completed work is documented as it is actually tested; planned concepts remain explicitly separated from verified results.
